Reprint source note (p. 32): 'Word 3:3 (1947), 155-172'; original Word pagination of sec. 7.1 not verified (T&F 403). Molinos rule: SPA vol. 1 p. 456, entry 875, paragraphs STRESS and INTONATION; the SPA header names the basis 'Hunter, Georgia G. and Eunice V. Pike 1969.. Linguistics 47.24-40, informant, 2 years'. Dyk & Stoudt 1973: 118 (Apendice I.B 'El Guion') of the 1973 facsimile.
catalog_quote: 7.1. Every Mixteco morpheme in its full form consists of one of the following bisyllabic sequences (C represents a consonant, V a vowel, n nasalization of final vowel): CVCV, CVʔCV, CVV, CVʔV; CVCVn, CVVn, CVʔVn. ... The first syllable of any morpheme may optionally be marked by stress. The second syllable is never stressed. If the listener hears a stressed syllable he knows that he is at the beginning of a morpheme. The first syllable, nevertheless, is not necessarily stressed; frequently I can detect no extra intensity on it whatever. It is the morpheme unit which controls these two optional phenomena. When neither special length nor stress is present, the potential must still be symbolized by an indication of morpheme beginnings, since the reader without such symbolization would tend to make some syllables more intense than others but would frequently stress the wrong ones. ... The indication of potential initial stress and potential medial lengthening is complicated by the phenomenon of morpheme reduction, by which the basic two-syllable form is reduced to a monosyllabic proclitic or enclitic that attaches to another full morpheme. ... To place a stress mark at the beginning of every morpheme would misrepresent the facts by insisting on a feature that is frequently absent. [p. 48] The morpheme is marked by optional initial stress and optional length of medial consonant.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: sanm1295 is not in the catalog. Of the three title-hits: (1) Pike 1967 (To honor Roman Jakobson) is a general theory paper; archive.org full-text snippets show its only Mixtec material is an Acatlan upstep example and no SMG stress statement (full text lending-restricted; snippets saved) — low priority. (2) McKinnon & Prieto 2014 is a Catalan-lab impoliteness-perception study; Glottolog itself flags the mig link as a machine assignment from the word 'mock' — irrelevant. (3) Yip 1981 is an unpublished MIT ms. formalising Hunter & Pike 1969's Molinos tone-stress system; no copy found — low priority (the primary, Hunter & Pike 1969 Linguistics 47, remains paywalled). Chasing Pike led to an OPEN scan of Brend (ed.) 1972 Selected Writings (archive.org, unrestricted), which reprints Pike 1947 'Grammatical prerequisites to phonemic analysis' (Word 3) with a first-hand SMG statement, pp. 44-45: stress, when present, is on the first syllable of the bisyllabic morpheme, never the second, and is optional/demarcative. Crossref, Glottolog and archive.org APIs worked.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is determined by tone sequences and the location of the stem (couplet) according to the following rules. The last high tone (or last mid, if there is no high) which is followed by a lower tone is stressed, provided this stress does not occur before the stem. Words with all high or all mid tones have equal stress on all syllables. Words with all low tones, or rising tone sequences, stress the first stem syllable. But if sequences of two high or two mid tones are preceded by a lower tone, there is a slight lengthening (marked as stress) of the vowel with the lower tone. Note that this word stress is different from phrase stress. (See intonation.) (p. 25)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Molinos (San Pedro Molinos) Mixtec is a three-tone language in which word stress is tone-conditioned within the phonological word built on the disyllabic stem ('couplet'): stress goes to the last H-toned (else last M-toned) syllable that precedes a lower tone, never to a pre-stem syllable; if no such fall exists (all-L or rising sequences) stress defaults to the first syllable of the stem/couplet; level all-H or all-M words have no single prominent syllable. de Lacy (1999: 25-26) restates the same page as: rightmost H before M/L, else rightmost M before L, else leftmost syllable, with duration and raised pitch as correlates (Hunter & Pike 1969: 25).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; SPA notes only a 'slight lengthening (marked as stress)' on a lower-toned vowel preceding HH or MM sequences.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress never falls on pre-stem (pre-couplet) syllables; all-high or all-mid words have equal stress on all syllables; phrase stress is separate: 'Phrase stress falls on the last syllable, unless it has the form /h, glottal stop/ + V, in which case it is prefinal' (SPA p. 456, INTONATION, from Hunter & Pike 1969). For San Miguel el Grande proper, Dyk & Stoudt (1973: 118) add only that an enclitic 'conserva su propio acento'.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (couplet nucleus plus pre-/post-couplet syllables) for word stress; phonological phrase for phrase-final phrase stress. Statement describes the Molinos dialect (sanp1259), read second-hand; primary p. 25 not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit stress rule I could read (second-hand, via SPA 1979 and de Lacy 1999) is Hunter & E. V. Pike 1969 on MOLINOS Mixtec = San Pedro Molinos, Glottolog dialect sanp1259 under sanm1295 (Glottolog lists this article among sanm1295's references; the archive.org SPA sheet is even filed under 'mig'). For San Miguel el Grande proper the primary descriptions are K. Pike 1944/1948 and Mak 1953 (not accessible); Dyk & Stoudt 1965/1973 (read) only says enclitics keep their own accent. For Chalcatongo (sanm1296) the primary is Macaulay 1996 (not accessible); Macaulay 1987 (read) gives no stress placement. McKendry 2013's claims about 'MIG' stress are her own metrical reanalysis of Pike/Mak data, not a field report.

new_statements.reading: First-hand fieldworker statement for San Miguel el Grande Mixteco: the native morpheme is bisyllabic (CVCV, CVʔCV, CVV, CVʔV and nasalized variants), and stress, when it occurs, is fixed on the FIRST syllable of that bisyllabic morpheme (couplet); the second syllable is never stressed. Stress is demarcative and optional (often phonetically absent), not an obligatory culminative word accent. Consistent with McKendry 2013's reanalysis (initial syllable of the disyllabic word) already held by the project, and with the SPA 1979 second-hand summary of Molinos (default first stem syllable), but this is the only primary-source SMG statement obtained so far.

readall_conflicts: The standing tension in the record remains as before: Pike 1947 (first-hand, San Miguel el Grande proper) describes optional demarcative stress on the FIRST syllable of the bisyllabic morpheme/couplet, second syllable never stressed; the SPA 1979 summary of Hunter & Pike 1969:25 (San Pedro Molinos dialect, sanp1259 under sanm1295) states a tone-conditioned word-stress rule (last high, or last mid if no high, followed by a lower tone is stressed, not before the stem; default otherwise). These are different varieties and different analytical framings rather than a flat contradiction; Longacre 1957 could not be read to arbitrate.

sources.note: Reconstructs Proto-Mixtec 'tonemic couplets' with two registers (*high, *low) plus a sandhi-only *modified tone and couplet-final glottal stop; SMG and Molinos are 'area A' dialects whose morphemes that perturb a following couplet to high continue Proto-Mixtec glottal-final couplets; SMG's special noun-modifier perturbation (Pike 1948: 82-87) is derived from a deleted relative marker; reflex tables give SMG/Molinos correspondences (e.g. SM high-low ~ Mol high-mid, note 11).

sources.note: 'I created a database of tonal and segmental sound changes across a sample of 42 Mixtec languages. I calculated phylogenetic signal with the metric D and estimated rates of change with a hidden Markov model.. the majority of tone changes show phylogenetic signal and.. they generally do not change at a faster rate than segments.'
